paper_sections.title: Neural correlates of metacognitive systematic bias
The different cognitive mechanisms between overestimated bias and underestimated bias
Dissociable neural networks supporting metacognitive systematic bias

description.value: An fMRI study of the neural mechanisms underlying overestimated and underestimated metacognitive systematic bias during encoding and immediate judgments of learning for abstract word pairs, using univariate GLM, multivariate pattern analysis, and effective connectivity analysis.

spans.text: In this study, we utilized judgments of learning task in human participants to compare the neural mechanism difference in metacognitive systematic bias.

description.value: fMRI data were converted from DICOM to NIFTI, initial images were discarded, slice-timing correction, realignment, coregistration, normalization to the Montreal Neurological Institute template, resampling, and spatial smoothing were performed.

spans.text: First, all the EPI DICOM data were converted to NIFTI format. The first three images from each run were automatically discarded by the scanner to allow scanner equilibrium. Second, all volume slice scan times were corrected to the middle time slice and realigned to the first scan to correct for head motion. Third, the structural images of each subject were coregistered with the mean functional images, and then the images were normalized to the Montreal Neurological Institute template. Fourth, all voxels were resampled to 3 × 3 × 3 mm. Last, all functional volumes were smoothed by using an 8-mm FWHM isotropic Gaussian kernel.

name.value: encoding and immediate judgments of learning task

spans.text: In the scanner and each run, participants performed an encoding and immediate judgment of learning (JOLs) task.

description.value: Participants encoded abstract word pairs and immediately judged how likely they were to remember the unseen target word in a later recognition test.

spans.text: After encoding each pair, participants saw one word from the pair (the cue) on the screen and were asked to predict how likely they would remember the unseen target in the post-scan recognition task on a four-point scale, with 1 indicating “will be absolutely forgotten” and 4 indicating “will be absolutely remembered”.
